items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: What distinguishes the major Buddhist schools?

options.text: There are no real differences between Buddhist schools

Theravada ('teaching of the elders', dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos) emphasises individual liberation through the Pali Canon; Mahayana (East Asia, Vietnam) emphasises the bodhisattva path and includes Pure Land, Zen and Tibetan (Vajrayana) traditions
Theravada is Buddhist; Mahayana is a separate religion

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal (the awakened practitioner).

Tibetan Buddhism is sometimes treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. Theravada and Mahayana share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the texts treated as authoritative, and the role of devotion.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) has three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). Tanakh is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in a one-year cycle (annual cycle) or three-year cycle (some Reform congregations). The annual cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' as a generic term for Jewish scripture obscures structure. Students need to distinguish Torah, Tanakh and Talmud — and notice that Christian 'Old Testament' is the same content as Tanakh but in different order.
